title: The Preterite --- Your First Past Tense

lessons.title: ayer — the word that opens the past

segments.text: Everything you have said so far happens now or later. This lesson gives you the one word that points the other way — backwards — and warns you what the verbs in this chapter are about to do.
voy a + infinitive — you can already point forwards; this points back.
vowel-a, vowel-e — two syllables, stress on the last: a-YÉR (ah-YEHR). see reference.
ayer — "yesterday." It is two Latin words that fused:
ad + heri becomes ayer (to) (yesterday) (yesterday).

Latin heri is the same ancient word as English yesterday and German gestern. The h- fell silent and then fell away, the -ri softened to a -y- sound, and ad heri — "to yesterday" — packed down into one short word.

Ayer is a time frame: a word that tells the listener when, before the verb ever gets a chance to. That matters more than it looks, because Spanish will not let a past time frame sit beside a present verb. Say ayer and the verb must follow you backwards.
That is what the rest of this chapter is for. Spanish has two past tenses, and they split the past between them:

utterances: preterite. what it says: it happened, and it finished. met in: this chapter.
imperfect. what it says: it was going on, or it used to happen. met in: a later chapter.

segments.text: English blurs this — "I spoke" covers both. Spanish makes you choose, every time. You do not have to choose yet; you only need to know that the choice is coming, so the next few lessons do not look like arbitrary endings.

segments.instruction: which of the two past tenses is for something finished?
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which of the two past tenses is for something finished?]

segments.text: Which two Latin words gave us ayer? (Ad and heri.) English keeps heri inside which word? (Yesterday.) How many past tenses does Spanish have? (Two — one for finished, one for ongoing.)

lessons.title: fui — one past set shared by ser and ir
lessons.gloss: the shared singular preterite of ser and ir — fui, fuiste, fue

segments.text: You already use ser for identity and ir for going. Spanish now gives both verbs one completed-past set. This lesson keeps the same three singular persons you know: fui, fuiste, fue.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: three singular forms, two verbs

headers: completed past of ser or ir
utterances: person: yo. completed past of ser or ir: fui.
person: tú. completed past of ser or ir: fuiste.
person: él / ella / usted. completed past of ser or ir: fue.

segments.text: Say fui, fuiste, fue. Each form can belong to either verb. The surrounding words decide which meaning is possible:
Fui a Madrid. — “I went to Madrid.” The known a plus a destination points to ir.
Fue Roberto. — “It was Roberto.” Identification points to ser.
Fui and fue are one-syllable words, so standard Spanish spelling gives them no written accent. Plural forms wait until a later lesson.

The shared set continues the Latin perfect family of “be,” including Latin fuī, “I have been.” Sound change and analogy reshaped the inherited forms. Spanish ir then came to share this past family with ser: a case of suppletion, where one verb draws forms from more than one historical root. English go / went uses the same broad strategy, although not the same words.

segments.prompt: Give the shared singular preterite forms of ser and ir: yo, tú, then él/ella/usted.

feedback.incorrect: Retrieve only the three learned singular forms: fui, fuiste, fue.

segments.prompt: Say 'I went to Madrid' in Spanish.

feedback.incorrect: Use the shared yo form fui, then known a plus Madrid.

segments.prompt: In 'Fue Roberto', which verb does fue express?

feedback.correct: Right: identifying Roberto points to ser.
feedback.incorrect: This sentence identifies who it was, so fue expresses ser.

segments.text: Give the three shared forms. (Fui, fuiste, fue.) Which two verbs share them? (Ser and ir.) What decides the meaning? (Context.) What older family supplied the forms? (The Latin perfect family of “be.”) Next, reuse the known verb hablar to build a regular singular past.

lessons.title: hablé — a regular singular past from a known verb
lessons.gloss: the regular singular -ar preterite — hablé, hablaste, habló

segments.text: You know hablar and its present singular hablo, hablas, habla. To say that the speaking was completed, keep habl- and learn three new endings: hablé, hablaste, habló.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: present beside completed past

utterances: person: yo. present: hablo. completed past: hablé.
person: tú. present: hablas. completed past: hablaste.
person: él / ella / usted. present: habla. completed past: habló.

segments.text: Say hablé, hablaste, habló. This is a complete singular pattern, not a preview of plural forms. Notice the exact changes:
hablo becomes hablé changes the final vowel and moves stress to the end.
hablas becomes hablaste adds the past ending -aste.
habla becomes habló changes the final vowel and moves stress to the end.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: two accents, one natural stress pattern

segments.text: The written accents in hablé and habló show final stress. Without those marks, words ending in a vowel normally stress the next-to-last syllable. Hablaste already follows that ordinary pattern — blas is next to last — so it needs no written accent. The mark records the stress; it is not the only change that makes a form past.
Now reuse known words:
Hablé español. — “I spoke Spanish.”
¿Hablaste español? — “Did you speak Spanish?”
Habló español. — “He, she, or you-formal spoke Spanish.”

The regular -ar past continues material from the Latin first-conjugation perfect, visible in forms such as amāvī, amāvistī, amāvit. Centuries of sound change and analogy produced the Spanish family -é, -aste, -ó. The history explains a family resemblance; it is not one tidy letter-by-letter erosion for every modern ending.

segments.instruction: “hablé and habló carry written accents; hablaste does not”
segments.source: [YOU SAY: “hablé and habló carry written accents; hablaste does not”]

segments.prompt: Give the singular completed-past forms of hablar: yo, tú, then él/ella/usted.

feedback.incorrect: Use hablé with its final written accent, then known español.

segments.prompt: Which form means 'I spoke' as a completed event: hablo or hablé?

feedback.correct: Right: hablé is the completed-past yo form.
feedback.incorrect: Hablo is present; hablé is the completed-past form.

segments.text: Give the three learned past forms. (Hablé, hablaste, habló.) Which two carry written accents, and why? (Hablé and habló; the marks show final stress.) What older family lies behind the endings? (The Latin first-conjugation perfect.) Next: choose between the two past patterns using only known words.

lessons.title: Practice — two singular ways to talk about a completed past
lessons.gloss: a singular checkpoint for fui/fuiste/fue and hablé/hablaste/habló

segments.text: This checkpoint adds nothing. Retrieve the shared singular set and the regular hablar set, then use context and spelling to keep them apart.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the complete frame for this chapter

segments.text: shared past of ser and ir: fui, fuiste, fue.
regular past of hablar: hablé, hablaste, habló.
context: Fui a Madrid expresses ir; Fue Roberto expresses ser.
time contrast: Hablo español is present; Hablé español is completed past.
spelling: hablé and habló show final stress with a written accent; hablaste needs none.
Plural persons, additional past-tense verb classes, new time words, and new place or person vocabulary wait for later lessons.
The fui family continues Latin perfect “be” material and became shared by ser and ir. The regular -ar endings continue Latin first-conjugation perfect material, reshaped by sound change and analogy.

segments.prompt: Give the three learned forms shared by ser and ir.

feedback.incorrect: Retrieve the singular set: fui, fuiste, fue.

segments.prompt: Give the three learned completed-past forms of hablar.

feedback.incorrect: Retrieve the singular set: hablé, hablaste, habló.

segments.prompt: Which sentence uses the shared form as ir, 'to go': Fui a Madrid or Fue Roberto?

feedback.correct: Right: a plus Madrid supplies a destination, so fui expresses ir.
feedback.incorrect: The destination phrase a Madrid makes Fui a Madrid the ir sentence.

segments.prompt: Give 'I speak Spanish' and then 'I spoke Spanish.'

feedback.incorrect: Use present hablo first, then completed-past hablé.

segments.prompt: Which two of hablé, hablaste, habló carry written accents?

feedback.correct: Right: hablé and habló mark final stress.
feedback.incorrect: The final-stressed forms are hablé and habló.

segments.text: Give both singular sets. (Fui, fuiste, fue; hablé, hablaste, habló.) How does context separate ser from ir? (A destination points to going; identification points to being.) Which regular forms carry written accents? (Hablé and habló.) The next chapter can add another past family without borrowing plural forms or unseen vocabulary from this checkpoint.
